blocks.text: In Greek you would call this ψιλοῦν [psiloun]. Theophrastus, Historia Plantarum, book 4, chapter 16: Ἐν Μιλήτῳ δὲ τὰς ἐλαίας, ὅταν ὦσι περὶ τὸ ἀνθεῖν, κάμπαι κατεσθίουσιν; αἱ μὲν τὰ φύλλα, αἱ δὲ τὰ ἄνθη ἕτεραι τῷ γένει· καὶ ψιλοῦσι τὰ δένδρα [En Milētō de tas elaias, hotan ōsi peri to anthein, kampai katesthiousin; hai men ta phylla, hai de ta anthē heterai tō genei; kai psilousi ta dendra]. At Miletus caterpillars gnaw the olives when they are in flower, some the leaves, others, of a different kind, the flower, and so they strip the trees bare. But in Joel it follows that the branches of the fig tree turn white. It will seem that this cannot happen unless the bark is stripped off so that the sapwood is exposed, as was done by Jacob, Gen. XXX, 37. I reply that the bark of a tree itself turns white when it rots. Hence Theophrastus, De causis, book 5, chapter 12: Διὰ τὴν ἀτροφίαν ἐκλευκαίνεται καὶ ἀπόλλυται τὰ δένδρα [Dia tēn atrophian ekleukainetai kai apollytai ta dendra]; For lack of nourishment trees turn white and perish. That trees perish and wither at the touch of locusts will be shown below. However that may be, it is established from the histories of the Abyssinians that locusts cut off not only the bark but even the stems of shrubs, when they are reduced to a lack of other fodder ^{(3)}. So Scaliger asserts in the 192nd Exercitatio against Cardano.

[III, 297] Verse 9: The meal offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the Lord; the priests, the ministers of the Lord, mourn. [col. 470]] As in verse 13: Come, and spend the night in sackcloth; for the meal offering and the drink offering are withheld from the house of your God. From both these passages Abarbanel infers that the temple had then been destroyed by the Babylonians; whereas the contrary follows, namely that the temple was standing. For a sacrifice cannot be cut off or withheld from a house that no longer exists.

Verse 10: The field is laid waste, the land mourns; for the grain is laid waste, the new wine has blushed, the oil languishes.] From these the firstfruits and tithes were offered to the Lord, Num. XVIII, 12. Deut. XIV, 23. and XVIII, 3. 4. And from the same the meal offerings and drink offerings were made. So when these three were lacking, there was nothing from which the customary oblations could be made. The land is said to mourn, as among the Hebrews is said of whatever has been laid waste and made desolate and changed for the worse. So Es. XXIV, 7: The new wine mourns, the vine languishes. Thren. II, 8: He made the rampart and the wall mourn; they languished together. By the same figure the oil is said to languish and the new wine to blush (as the vine in verse 12), as though affected with shame because they cannot meet the expectation of men. Thus Es. XXXIII, 9: The land mourned and languished, Lebanon blushed. To the mourning land is opposed a field glad with crops and fodder in Sallust, Histories, book 2, and glad crops in the Poet. Hence too the dung with which fields are manured is commonly called laetamen, as Servius writes, which in Italian is letame.

Verse 11: Be ashamed, O farmers; wail, O vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley; because the harvest of the field has perished. 12. The vine has blushed, etc.] The order would be: "Be ashamed, O farmers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. Wail, O vinedressers, because the vine has blushed." But these are transposed by a figure such as the χιασμός [chiasmos]. Such is that said of the church, Cant. I, 4. (var. 5.): I am black, but comely, as the tents of Kedar, and the curtains of Solomon. That is, "Outwardly, and in the [III, 298] judgement of men, I am black, like the haircloth tents of the Kedarenes; but comely inwardly, and before God, like the magnificent curtains of Solomon." So there is a like μετάθεσις [metathesis].

Verse 12: The vine has blushed, and the fig tree languishes. The pomegranate too, the palm, and the apple tree, all the trees of the field have withered, because joy has perished from the sons of men. That is, the joy they feel at harvest and vintage, and when the fruits of the trees are gathered. Hence Es. IX, 3: They have rejoiced before you with the joy that is at harvest. And Psal. IV, 8: You have put greater gladness in my heart than at the time when their grain and new wine abounded. Although it is plain that these verses concern the damage inflicted by locusts on the crops of the land and the fruits of the trees, Abarbanel nevertheless found something to object. Namely, that if the matter concerned locusts, it would be pointless to say that the vine, the fig tree and all the trees of the field had withered, since locusts consume the fruit but do not harm the trees themselves in the least. From this it is clear that this plague was little known to him. For Pliny writes that the locust scorches many things by its touch. And Pisides in the Creation of the World:
Τήκει τὰ δένδρα, καὶ μαραίνει τὴν πόαν, [Tēkei ta dendra, kai marainei tēn poan,]
